771.title: A double portion (2 Kings 2:1–15)
771.hook: Elijah rises in a whirlwind; Elisha picks up his mantle
771.howItsDone: Jews remember Elijah at the Passover seder with a cup poured for him, and the song Eliyahu HaNavi, asking for his return, is sung at the end of Shabbat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, in Naboth's vineyard, Elijah met the king with one question: hast thou killed, and taken? Did you say a true word for someone wronged? Today is Elijah's last day on earth, and someone refuses to leave his side. Day seven hundred seventy-one.

Everyone seems to know what's about to happen. Elijah and his student Elisha are walking from Gilgal, and Elijah says: stay here, the Lord has sent me on to Beth-el. Elisha answers with an oath: as the Lord lives, I will not leave thee. At Beth-el, a group of prophets comes out and asks Elisha, do you know the Lord will take your master today? Yes, I know, he says. Hold your peace. Then Jericho: the same request, the same oath, another band of prophets, the same answer. Then the Jordan. Elisha simply will not be sent away.
screen: `STAY HERE.` → `I WILL NOT LEAVE THEE.` → `HOLD YOUR PEACE.`

segments.voice: At the Jordan, Elijah takes off his mantle, his rough prophet's cloak, rolls it up, and strikes the water. The river divides, and the two of them cross on dry ground. On the other side Elijah turns to his student. Ask what I shall do for thee, before I am taken. And Elisha asks: "let a double portion of thy spirit be upon me." In Israel's inheritance law, the firstborn son received a double share. Some readers hear Elisha asking to be the heir, the one who carries on the household. Some Jewish commentators also read it more literally, as twice his teacher's wonders. Elijah answers honestly: thou hast asked a hard thing. If you see me when I'm taken, it will be so. If not, it won't. And as they walk and talk, a chariot of fire and horses of fire separate them, and Elijah goes up by a whirlwind into heaven. Elisha sees it, and cries out: my father, my father, the chariot of Israel and the horsemen thereof. Then he tears his own clothes in two. Grief first. And then he bends down and picks up the mantle that fell from Elijah. He walks back to the Jordan. He strikes the water with that same cloak and asks, where is the Lord, the God of Elijah? The water divides again. The prophets watching from Jericho say: the spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha. Notice that the inheritance doesn't arrive as a feeling. It arrives as an old cloak lying on the ground, and a river that still has to be crossed. In Jewish tradition Elijah never quite leaves the story: tradition says he will return to announce redemption, and a cup is poured for him at the Passover seder.
screen: `I WILL NOT LEAVE THEE.` · `THE FIRSTBORN'S SHARE.` · then, large: `A DOUBLE PORTION OF THY SPIRIT.` · then: `THE MANTLE ON THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: carry on someone's good work. Let your hands rest open in your lap. Think of someone who taught you, cared for you, or started something good and then moved on, or passed on: a grandparent, a teacher, a friend, a neighbor. What did they do that you admired? Name one piece of it. A way of welcoming people, a recipe, a habit of calling on the lonely, a craft. That's the mantle on the ground. Then choose how to pick it up: one small way you could carry that work forward this week. If you pray, you can remember them by name. The bell holds the time.
A double portion. Elisha's request as Elijah was taken: the heir's share of his teacher's spirit, to carry the work on. Today's word.
Your line: a double portion. Today, pick up one piece of good work someone left you, and do it once, in their honor. Day seven hundred seventy-one.

options: that he stay a little longer.
a double portion of his spirit.
his blessing on your travels.
fork.reveal: Elisha asks for a double portion of his spirit. Elijah says it's a hard thing: if you see me taken, it will be so.

what it means: Elisha asks to carry on his teacher's work, and then has to pick up the cloak himself.
what a scholar hears: pi shnayim is the firstborn's share in Deuteronomy 21:17; some Jewish commentators also read it as twice Elijah's wonders.

772.title: The Shunammite (2 Kings 4:8–37)
772.hook: a woman builds the prophet a room and asks nothing: "I dwell among mine own people"
772.howItsDone: Jews read the story of the Shunammite as a haftarah alongside the Torah reading of Abraham's welcome to his guests, and welcoming guests, hachnasat orchim, is honored as a mitzvah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Elisha asked for a double portion and picked up Elijah's mantle from the ground. Did you carry on a piece of someone's good work? Today, Elisha is on the road, and a woman in the town of Shunem notices him. Day seven hundred seventy-two.

A bed, a table, a stool and a lamp. That's the whole list, and the text gives it item by item. A woman in Shunem, described as a great woman, has been inviting the traveling prophet Elisha to eat whenever he passes through. Then she goes further. She says to her husband: this is a holy man of God who keeps passing by. Let's build him a small room on the roof, with a bed, a table, a stool and a lamp, so whenever he comes, he has a place to rest. No one asked her to. She saw a traveler who kept passing by, and made room.
screen: `A MEAL WHENEVER HE PASSES.` → `A SMALL ROOM ON THE ROOF.` → `A BED, A TABLE, A STOOL, A LAMP.`

segments.voice: One day Elisha is resting in that room, and he wants to repay her. He sends his servant Gehazi with an offer. You've taken all this trouble for us. What can be done for you? Shall we speak for you to the king, or to the captain of the army? It's a real offer. A word from a prophet in the right ear could open doors. And her answer is quiet and complete: "I dwell among mine own people." Thank you, but I'm fine. I live among my own people. She isn't looking for a connection at court. Her hospitality wasn't an investment. Elisha doesn't let it go, though. Gehazi points out that she has no son, and her husband is old. So Elisha calls her and tells her: about this season next year, you will hold a son. Her reply is startling: no, my lord, do not lie to your handmaid. She had never asked for it. And the son is born. The story doesn't stop there. When the child has grown, he goes out to his father in the field and cries, my head, my head. He is carried to his mother, and dies on her lap. She carries him up to the little room, lays him on the prophet's bed, shuts the door, and rides straight to find Elisha. Asked on the way whether all is well, she says only: it is well. Then at Elisha's feet the grief pours out. Elisha comes, prays, stretches himself over the child, and the boy sneezes and opens his eyes. And look where the miracle happens: in the room she built for a stranger. The space she made out of kindness, asking nothing, became the place where her son was given back to her.
screen: `WHAT CAN BE DONE FOR THEE?` · then, large: `I DWELL AMONG MINE OWN PEOPLE.` · then: `DO NOT LIE TO THY HANDMAID.` · `THE PROPHET'S ROOM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make space for a guest. Look around the room you're in. Think of the spaces you have: a spare chair, a corner of a table, an hour on a weekend, a seat beside you at lunch. Then think of someone who passes through your life a little tired: a new coworker, a neighbor living alone, a relative who visits, a friend who's been quiet. What would the Shunammite's small room look like for them? It doesn't need to be big. A plate, a chair, a time to sit. Plan how you'd set it out, expecting nothing back. The bell holds the time.
The Shunammite. The woman of Shunem who built a small room for a traveling prophet and, offered a favor at court, said she dwelt among her own people. Today's word.
Your line: I dwell among my people. Today, make a little room for someone, a chair, a plate, a few minutes, and don't keep score. Day seven hundred seventy-two.

what it means: a woman makes room for a stranger, asks nothing, and the room becomes the place of her son's life.

773.title: Wash, and be clean (2 Kings 5:1–14)
773.hook: the general wanted something grand, and was told to wash in the Jordan
773.howItsDone: Jews read Naaman's healing as part of the book of Kings and as a haftarah alongside the Torah's laws of skin disease, which are read in the book of Leviticus.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Shunammite built a small room for a stranger and turned down a favor at court: I dwell among my people. Did you make a little room for someone? Today, someone arrives at Elisha's door with horses and chariots. Day seven hundred seventy-three.

Horses, chariots, servants, and gifts of silver, gold and fine clothing. Naaman, captain of the army of the king of Aram, has come a long way, and he has come in style. The text calls him a great man, honored by his king, a mighty man of valor. And then it adds a short phrase that undoes all of it: he was a leper. He has a skin disease no rank can cure. Someone has told him there's a prophet in Israel who could heal him. So the whole procession pulls up and stops at Elisha's door. And Elisha doesn't come out.
screen: `HORSES, CHARIOTS, SILVER, GOLD.` → `A GREAT MAN, BUT A LEPER.` → `ELISHA DOESN'T COME OUT.`

segments.voice: Instead, Elisha sends a messenger with a short instruction: go and wash in the Jordan seven times, and your flesh will be restored, and you will be clean. That's it. No ceremony. No prophet at the door. Naaman is furious, and the text lets us hear exactly why. He says, in effect: I thought he would surely come out to me, stand there, call on the name of his God, wave his hand over the spot, and heal me. He had pictured the whole scene in advance. And then the insult of the river itself. Are not Abana and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel? Couldn't I wash in them and be clean? He turns and leaves in a rage. What stops him is not the prophet. It's his own servants. They come near and call him, my father. If the prophet had asked you to do some great thing, wouldn't you have done it? "How much rather then, when he saith to thee, Wash, and be clean?" It's a sharp, kind question. Naaman was ready for difficulty. He was ready for a quest, a price, a drama worthy of a general. What he couldn't accept was something ordinary. A plain river. Seven dips. No prophet at the bank. And yet he goes down to the Jordan, dips himself seven times, just as the man of God said, and his flesh comes back like the flesh of a little child, and he is clean. Notice the turn. The cure was there from the first message. What stood in the way was Naaman's picture of how it should happen. The hard part wasn't the washing. It was getting down off the chariot.
screen: `GO AND WASH IN THE JORDAN.` · `I THOUGHT HE WOULD COME OUT.` · then, large: `WASH, AND BE CLEAN.` · then: `LIKE THE FLESH OF A LITTLE CHILD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: try the simple thing. Uncross your arms and breathe out slowly. Then name something you've been stuck on, waiting for a big solution: a tense relationship, a messy room, a health habit, a project you can't start. Now ask what Naaman's servants asked: if the answer were something grand, would I do it? Then what's the plain, ordinary step I keep stepping over? An apology. Ten minutes of tidying. A walk. A glass of water. A phone call. Name it to yourself. Then take that first step in your mind: down off the chariot. The bell holds the time.
Wash. The plain instruction a great general almost refused: go down into an ordinary river and dip, as the prophet said. Today's word.
Your line: wash, and be clean. Today, when you catch yourself waiting for a grand fix, try the simple thing first. Day seven hundred seventy-three.

what it means: the cure was simple from the start; Naaman's pride had to come down first.
what a scholar hears: Naaman scripted the miracle in advance: I thought, he will surely come out to me.

774.title: The captive girl (2 Kings 5:2–3)
774.hook: an Israelite servant girl points her master toward healing
774.howItsDone: Jews read the captive girl's words at the start of Naaman's story in the book of Kings, which is read in synagogue as a haftarah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a great general almost refused the plain instruction: wash, and be clean. Did you try the simple thing? Today we go back to the start of that story, to the person who sent him to the prophet at all. Day seven hundred seventy-four.

She gets only a few lines. No name, no age, no words about her family. Raiding bands from Aram had gone into the land of Israel, and among what they carried off was a young girl. Now she works in a foreign house, waiting on the wife of the commander of the army whose raiders took her. That commander is Naaman. Everything we heard yesterday, the chariots, the gifts, the journey to Elisha's door, the river, begins with something this girl says to her mistress.
screen: `A FEW LINES, NO NAME.` → `CARRIED OFF BY RAIDERS.` → `SERVING IN NAAMAN'S HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Here is what she says, in the King James words: "Would God my lord were with the prophet that is in Samaria! for he would recover him of his leprosy." Read that slowly and look at who she's talking about. My lord. The man whose soldiers took her from her home. And her wish is for him to be healed. The text doesn't tell us what she felt. It doesn't say whether she was afraid, or homesick, or angry. It doesn't explain her motives at all. It only gives us the sentence, and the sentence is generous. Then notice how far that sentence travels. Word of it goes up the household: thus and thus said the maid from the land of Israel. It reaches the king of Aram, and he writes a letter to the king of Israel. Armies and kings and letters start moving, all because a servant girl spoke up. The next verses say the king of Israel panics when he reads the letter, tearing his clothes and asking, am I God, to kill and to make alive? The king doesn't think of the prophet. The girl did. She knew there was a prophet in Samaria, and she trusted he could help. Two more things stand out. First, she points away from herself. She doesn't claim any power. She simply knows where help can be found. Second, the story never mentions her again. No reward, no freedom, no thanks recorded. Naaman comes home healed, and the text has already moved on. But the healing began with her one sentence. It came from someone with no power at all, and the text bothered to keep it.
screen: `WOULD GOD MY LORD WERE WITH THE PROPHET.` · `THE SENTENCE TRAVELS TO KINGS.` · then, large: `A SMALL GIRL'S WORD.` · then: `NEVER MENTIONED AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be kind to someone who wronged you. This one is hard, so go gently. Sit still for a moment. Think of someone who hurt you in a small or middle-sized way. Not the deepest wound; something you can hold for two minutes. You don't have to excuse what they did. Just ask the girl's question: is there one good thing I could wish for this person? Healing, rest, a better day. Let that wish sit for a few breaths. If it won't come, that's honest too; simply notice it. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayers. The bell holds the time.
The captive girl. A young Israelite taken by raiders, serving in Naaman's house, whose one sentence sent her master to be healed. Today's word.
Your line: a small girl's word. Today, wish one person who wronged you something good, even quietly, and see if a kind word can find its way out. Day seven hundred seventy-four.

what it means: a captive with no power wishes healing on her captor, and her word sets kings in motion.
what a scholar hears: she is a na'arah ketanah, a little girl, beside Naaman the great man; healed, his flesh is like a little boy's.

775.title: Open his eyes (2 Kings 6:15–17)
775.hook: Elisha prays his servant will see the unseen help around them
775.howItsDone: Jews read the story of Elisha at Dothan as part of the book of Kings; Elisha's line that those with us are more than those with them is remembered as words of courage in frightening times.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a captive girl with no name spoke one generous sentence, and a small girl's word set kings in motion. Did you wish someone who wronged you something good? Today, Elisha's servant wakes up early and looks outside. Day seven hundred seventy-five.

Dawn in the town of Dothan. The servant of Elisha gets up early, steps out, and stops. An army has surrounded the city in the night: horses, chariots, a great host. The king of Aram has been at war with Israel, and again and again, the text says not once nor twice, Elisha warns the king of Israel where the ambush is. So the king of Aram has sent a whole army to capture one prophet. The servant runs back inside. His words are pure panic: "Alas, my master! how shall we do?"
screen: `DAWN IN DOTHAN.` → `AN ARMY AROUND THE CITY.` → `ALAS, MY MASTER!`

segments.voice: Elisha's answer is calm, and at first it sounds impossible: "Fear not: for they that be with us are more than they that be with them." More? The servant can see an army outside, and on his side, one prophet. Elisha doesn't argue with him. He doesn't explain. He prays, and his prayer is one short line: "LORD, I pray thee, open his eyes, that he may see." Notice what he does not ask for. He doesn't ask for the army to disappear, or for rescue, or for fire from heaven. He asks for his servant to see. And the text says the Lord opened the eyes of the young man, "and, behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire round about Elisha." The help had been there the whole time. Nothing outside changed. The servant changed. A few days ago a chariot of fire parted Elijah from his student. Now chariots of fire surround that student, and Elisha knew it before anyone saw them. Then the story takes a surprising turn. Elisha prays again, this time that the enemy soldiers be struck with blindness, and he leads them, confused, right into Samaria, to the king of Israel. The king of Israel asks, shall I strike them? Elisha says no. Set bread and water before them, let them eat and drink, and send them home. And the text says the raiding bands of Aram came no more into the land of Israel. So the chapter is about two kinds of sight. The servant learns to see help he couldn't see. And Israel's king is asked to see enemies as hungry men who could be fed. In both cases, the first change happens in someone's eyes.
screen: `MORE ARE WITH US.` · `NOT RESCUE: SIGHT.` · then, large: `OPEN HIS EYES.` · then: `BREAD FOR THE ENEMY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for help you haven't noticed. Start with whatever feels like an army around your city today: a deadline, a worry, a stretch of loneliness. Feel how big it is. Then, like the servant, look again at what is already around you. The chair holding you up, built by someone you'll never meet. Water you can drink. The light you're sitting in. Bread someone baked before dawn. A name in your phone you could call tonight. Let each one come into view, one at a time, like horses on a hillside. The bell holds the time.
Open his eyes. Elisha's prayer for his frightened servant: not that the army vanish, but that he see the help already there. Today's word.
Your line: more are with us. Today, when you feel surrounded, name one source of help you'd stopped seeing, and thank them if you can. Day seven hundred seventy-five.

776.title: Four lepers (2 Kings 7:3–9)
776.hook: outcasts find the enemy camp empty and decide to share the news
776.howItsDone: Jews read the story of the four lepers as a haftarah alongside the Torah's laws for healing from skin disease in Leviticus.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Elisha's servant saw the mountain full of chariots of fire, and heard: more are with us. Did you notice help you'd stopped seeing? Today, the city of Samaria is under siege and starving, and help comes from the people standing outside the gate. Day seven hundred seventy-six.

Outside the gate of Samaria sit four men with a skin disease. The law keeps them outside the city, and the city is under siege by the army of Aram, with famine inside. They do the math out loud: "Why sit we here until we die?" If we go into the city, there's famine, and we die there. If we sit here, we die here. So let's go over to the enemy camp. If they spare us, we live. If they kill us, we were dying anyway. At twilight, the four outcasts get up and walk toward the enemy.
screen: `FOUR MEN OUTSIDE THE GATE.` → `WHY SIT WE HERE UNTIL WE DIE?` → `WALKING TOWARD THE ENEMY.`

segments.voice: They reach the edge of the camp, and there's no one there. The text explains: the Lord had made the army of Aram hear a noise of chariots and horses, the noise of a great host, and they fled in the twilight, leaving their tents, their horses, their donkeys, everything. So the four men walk into an empty camp full of food. They go into one tent, eat and drink, and carry off silver and gold and clothing, and hide it. Then another tent, and they hide that too. Who could blame them? They've been hungry and shut out for who knows how long. And then they stop. One of them says: "We do not well: this day is a day of good tidings, and we hold our peace." Consider who's saying this. These are the men the law kept outside the walls, with famine on the other side of the gate. And yet they're the ones who realize that good news kept to yourself goes bad. They even admit a plain worry: if we wait until morning light, some trouble will come upon us. So they go back in the dark, call to the gatekeepers, and tell them: we came to the camp of Aram, and there was no one there, only horses tied, and donkeys tied, and the tents as they were. The king is suspicious at first and thinks it's a trap. Scouts go out, find a trail of clothes and gear all the way to the Jordan, and come back. And the starving city walks out and eats. The good news came from the edge, from four people nobody expected to hear from. And it reached the city because they decided a full stomach wasn't enough. A day of good tidings has to be told.
screen: `WHY SIT WE HERE UNTIL WE DIE?` · `AN EMPTY CAMP FULL OF FOOD.` · then, large: `WE DO NOT WELL.` · then: `GOOD NEWS FROM THE EDGE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: share good news today. Take one breath in and a longer one out, and ask yourself: what good thing do I know that someone else doesn't? A job opening a friend could use. A thank-you you never passed on. Praise for someone's work that you said behind their back but never to their face. A bit of hopeful news a worried person would want to hear. Let one come to mind. Now bring to mind the person who needs it, and how you'll tell them: a message, a call, a word in passing. Hold it ready, like the four men at the gate in the dark. The bell holds the time.
Four lepers. Outcasts at the gate of a starving city who found the enemy camp empty and decided they couldn't keep the news to themselves. Today's word.
Your line: a day of good tidings. Today, share one piece of good news with someone who needs to hear it, before the day is out. Day seven hundred seventy-six.

777.title: The north falls (2 Kings 17)
777.hook: Assyria takes Samaria and the northern tribes are carried away and scattered
777.howItsDone: Jews read 2 Kings 17 as part of the Former Prophets, and the hope that the scattered tribes will one day be gathered appears in the prophets and in Jewish prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, four outcasts at a city gate found an empty camp and said: this day is a day of good tidings, and we hold our peace. Did you pass some good news along? Today, the news is the opposite. Day seven hundred seventy-seven.

Look back over this week. Elisha asks for a double portion, and his teacher's cloak falls to him. A woman in Shunem builds a little room on her roof for a holy man. A proud general is told to wash in the Jordan, because a captive girl spoke up. A frightened servant has his eyes opened to help he couldn't see. Four lepers carry good news to a starving city. All of it happens in the northern kingdom, Israel, with its capital at Samaria. And today, in one chapter, that kingdom ends.
screen: `A WEEK IN THE NORTH.` → `CLOAK, ROOF, RIVER, GATE.` → `TODAY IT ENDS.`

segments.voice: The last king of the north is named Hoshea. He stops paying tribute to Assyria and looks to Egypt for help. The king of Assyria marches in, besieges Samaria, and takes it. Then he carries the people of Israel away into Assyria, and settles them in distant places the text names: Halah, and Habor by the river of Gozan, and the cities of the Medes. And then the chapter does something unusual. It stops telling the story and starts explaining it. Why did this happen? The writer's answer is long and blunt: the people had turned to other gods, though prophets had warned them again and again. The text says the Lord had warned Israel and Judah by every prophet and every seer, saying turn from your evil ways. They would not hear. And then one sad line: "there was none left but the tribe of Judah only." The north is gone. Next the king of Assyria brings in people from other lands to live in the empty towns of Samaria. The map is redrawn. Those carried away never come back in the story. The book of Kings simply goes on with Judah. Later readers would call them the lost tribes, and tradition tells stories about where they went. The prophets didn't let the north be forgotten, though. Ezekiel is told to take two sticks, one for Judah and one for Joseph, and join them into one in his hand. Jewish tradition keeps that hope alive: one day, the scattered come home. The lost tribes are lost to the record. They were not lost to memory.
screen: `HOSHEA TURNS TO EGYPT.` · `SAMARIA TAKEN, ISRAEL CARRIED AWAY.` · then, large: `NONE LEFT BUT THE TRIBE OF JUDAH.` · then: `THE STORY GOES SILENT.` · `TWO STICKS JOINED IN ONE HAND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of those lost to history. Let your shoulders drop. Bring to mind people whose names nobody wrote down: great-great-grandparents you can't name, a town that isn't on the map anymore, the workers who built a place you walk past every day. You don't need faces or details. Just let them be real for a moment. People who cooked, worried, laughed, and were carried off by time. With each slow breath, hold one of them in mind. If you pray, you can remember them before God. The bell holds the time.
The north falls. Assyria takes Samaria, the northern kingdom is carried away, and only Judah is left in the story. Today's word.
Your line: the lost tribes. Today, ask an older relative or friend one name from the family you've never heard, and write it down. Day seven hundred seventy-seven.
